power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Cochlear implants work, but not equally.
After decades of cohort studies, the familiar predictors of outcome (age, duration of deafness, residual hearing, etiology) still leave most of the spread between patients unexplained.
Research on how the brain handles degraded speech, audiovisual cues and everyday sounds shows that implant outcome measures test the brain at least as much as the ear.
Yet candidacy assessment still examines the cochlea, the auditory nerve and inner-ear anatomy, and rarely the cognitive and structural state of the brain that must learn to use the device.

This article argues that undetected neural variability, including cognitive decline, hearing-related atrophy and incidental pathology in brains assumed to be normal, is a plausible and largely unmeasured contributor to the missing variance.
It proposes routine cognitive and volumetric phenotyping of implant candidates, and of the control groups against which they are judged.

Because the brain restores much of the degraded implant signal through its predictive mechanisms, the article also calls for a new line of work: the development of dedicated tests of predictive brain capacity, a measure currently absent from both candidacy assessment and outcome research.
Every cochlear implant clinic knows the patient who should have done well and did not.
The surgery was uneventful, the array was fully inserted, the fitting was unremarkable, and the audiological history predicted a good result.
A year later, open-set word recognition is still poor, and none of the usual explanations quite fits.
This is rather frequent.

In the largest multicentre analyses of adult implant outcome, the classic predictors (duration of severe-to-profound loss, age at implantation, age at onset, etiology, implant experience) were statistically significant, yet together they explained only a small fraction of the differences between patients (Blamey et al., 2013; Lazard et al., 2012).
text.formatted: In the largest multicentre analyses of adult implant outcome, the classic predictors (duration of severe-to-profound loss, age at implantation, age at onset, etiology, implant experience) were statistically significant, yet together they explained only a small fraction of the differences between patients <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Blamey et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Lazard et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Adding newer factors, such as residual hearing and device characteristics, helped without closing the gap, and the decline in performance with longer deafness was attributed to central reorganization rather than to the ear (Lazard et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Adding newer factors, such as residual hearing and device characteristics, helped without closing the gap, and the decline in performance with longer deafness was attributed to central reorganization rather than to the ear <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Lazard et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: That central processing shapes implant outcome is not in dispute; it is the premise of most work in the field, including the studies reviewed below.
The thesis here is narrower.
Research has treated the brain almost entirely as something deafness acts upon, through reorganization, plasticity and crossmodal takeover.

Variability that has nothing to do with deafness, such as baseline structural integrity, cognitive reserve and incidental pathology, is measured neither in candidates nor in the normal-hearing controls they are compared with.
Implant teams image the temporal bone and the auditory nerve, measure residual hearing, and screen general fitness for surgery.
Cognitive testing is not a standard part of candidacy in most programmes, and where brain MRI is acquired, it is read for surgical contraindications rather than quantified.

Some share of the "unexplained" variance plausibly belongs to neural factors nobody measured: cognitive decline, hearing-related atrophy, and incidental structural anomalies in brains assumed to be normal.
Work on vocoded speech, audiovisual prediction, crossmodal interaction and sound categorization shows that implant outcome measures depend heavily on central processing.
The brains of implant candidates, and of the normal-hearing controls they are compared with, are less homogeneous than study designs assume.
Hearing loss is itself associated with structural change and cognitive decline, and cognition predicts outcome.
An important argument, to our knowledge not made before, concerns prediction.
The brain continually predicts incoming sensory information (Strelnikov, 2026), and we propose that much of what the implant fails to transmit is restored by predictive mechanisms of the brain.
text.formatted: The brain continually predicts incoming sensory information <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Strelnikov, 2026)</ref>, and we propose that much of what the implant fails to transmit is restored by predictive mechanisms of the brain.

text.text: Yet predictive capacity is measured neither in candidates nor in controls, and no dedicated test of it is in clinical use.
These are the main arguments we expose below.
A speech score after implantation looks like a measure of hearing.

It is better understood as the output of a chain of central operations: extracting structure from a spectrally impoverished signal, predicting what comes next, recruiting visual cues, and assigning meaning.

Our vocoding experiments in normal-hearing listeners have shown that acoustic degradation affects much of the temporal lobe uniformly, whereas the loss of intelligibility is reflected in specific posterior temporal regions; voice discrimination also survives degradation far better than word comprehension (Strelnikov et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Our vocoding experiments in normal-hearing listeners have shown that acoustic degradation affects much of the temporal lobe uniformly, whereas the loss of intelligibility is reflected in specific posterior temporal regions; voice discrimination also survives degradation far better than word comprehension <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Strelnikov et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: The same degraded input therefore yields different functional outcomes depending on which cortical network has to use it.
It was demonstrated that a speaker's facial expressions trigger a cortical response anticipating vocal emphasis before the corresponding sound arrives (Strelnikov et al., 2015).
text.formatted: It was demonstrated that a speaker's facial expressions trigger a cortical response anticipating vocal emphasis before the corresponding sound arrives <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Strelnikov et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In continuous speech, vision sets up a prediction of the auditory signal in the context of the phrase.
Real-world listening with an implant leans heavily on exactly this kind of top-down anticipation.

More generally, the brain continuously maintains and updates predictions about its environment; these predictions are shaped by past experience and embedded in the flow of neural activity, at rest as well as during tasks (Strelnikov, 2026).
text.formatted: More generally, the brain continuously maintains and updates predictions about its environment; these predictions are shaped by past experience and embedded in the flow of neural activity, at rest as well as during tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Strelnikov, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For an implant user, we argue, this predictive machinery is what restores the degraded signal: what the electrode array fails to transmit, the brain must supply from expectation.
Individual differences in predictive capacity are therefore likely to translate into differences in outcome.

Postlingually deaf implant users integrate auditory and visual speech more efficiently than normal-hearing listeners presented with comparably degraded sound, and they keep supra-normal speechreading for years after implantation (Rouger et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Postlingually deaf implant users integrate auditory and visual speech more efficiently than normal-hearing listeners presented with comparably degraded sound, and they keep supra-normal speechreading for years after implantation <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Rouger et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Visual and frontal activity shortly after activation predicts later speech recovery, whereas right superior temporal activity predicts it negatively (Strelnikov et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Visual and frontal activity shortly after activation predicts later speech recovery, whereas right superior temporal activity predicts it negatively <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Strelnikov et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: When implant users categorised the gender of voices paired with faces, they remained strongly influenced by the visual information even after maximal speech recovery, and even when compared with normal-hearing listeners at matched auditory performance (Barone et al., 2016).
text.formatted: When implant users categorised the gender of voices paired with faces, they remained strongly influenced by the visual information even after maximal speech recovery, and even when compared with normal-hearing listeners at matched auditory performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Barone et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Speech scores, in other words, can normalize while the underlying audiovisual architecture remains different from controls.
Children solve the problem differently.
Implanted children were shown to categorize everyday sounds much as normal-hearing peers do, despite poorer identification (Berland et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Implanted children were shown to categorize everyday sounds much as normal-hearing peers do, despite poorer identification <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Berland et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: But they relied more on acoustic features than on meaning for some sounds, and individual variation was considerable in both groups.
Categorization is a cognitive strategy layered on top of the auditory signal, and children differ in how they deploy it.
The common lesson is methodological.
Two patients with the same word score may have reached it through different central routes, and two patients with the same cochlea and device may reach very different scores.
Any variation in the integrity of the networks for prediction, multisensory integration, working memory and categorisation feeds directly into outcome variance.
If that variation is not measured, it is filed under noise.
If clinical history explains only a small part of outcome variance, where is the rest?
For twenty-five years, the dominant answer has been crossmodal reorganization: deafness rewires the auditory and visual cortices, and the nature of that rewiring sets the ceiling for recovery.
The imaging evidence is real, but it is inconsistent in direction and almost entirely interpreted through that single lens.

text.text: First, the same broad marker, visual involvement in speech processing, is linked to good outcome in some designs and poor outcome in others; the adaptive-versusmaladaptive debate has run for two decades without resolution.
Second, almost every predictive signal is read as a trace of deafness-induced reorganization.
Two results break that pattern, and they are the most interesting.
In young children, pre-surgical structural MRI was shown to predict speech improvement where age, residual hearing and demographics could not (Feng et al., 2018).

text.text: The informative tissue was not altered by deafness.

In adults with postlingual deafness, Han et al. (2019) concluded that the auditory cortex was relatively resistant to crossmodal change, and that traits in late visual processing and cognitive control seemed to be more reliable prognostic markers.

text.text: Both findings point to the same possibility.
Part of what predicts implant outcome may be the general integrity of the brain, independent of anything hearing loss did to it.
That is a different hypothesis from reorganization, and it calls for different measurements.
Study design adds a further twist.

In the paediatric MRI study, following standard practice, children with developmental delay, additional disabilities or gross brain malformation were excluded, and no implanted child showed acquired brain anomalies (Feng et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In the paediatric MRI study, following standard practice, children with developmental delay, additional disabilities or gross brain malformation were excluded, and no implanted child showed acquired brain anomalies <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Feng et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Such screening protects a study's internal validity.
It also means that the brains most likely to explain poor outcomes are often removed from the samples that try to explain them, while remaining in clinical caseloads.
Research designs treat "normal" as a property a participant either has or lacks.
Population imaging says otherwise.

A meaningful minority of people with no neurological complaint carry structural findings on MRI, and the proportion is higher in exactly the groups that fill implant clinics: young children with congenital hearing loss and adults over 60.

Large imaging studies of asymptomatic people consistently find clinically relevant incidental findings on a small but non-trivial share of scans, more often with high-resolution sequences, and silent vascular lesions become common with age (Morris et al., 2009; Vernooij et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Large imaging studies of asymptomatic people consistently find clinically relevant incidental findings on a small but non-trivial share of scans, more often with high-resolution sequences, and silent vascular lesions become common with age <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Morris et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Vernooij et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Young research volunteers are not exempt (Gur et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Young research volunteers are not exempt <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Gur et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: In paediatric implant candidates, brain abnormalities, mostly whitematter changes but also ventriculomegaly and other structural lesions, are common on pre-implant scans (Hong et al., 2010; Moon et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2015).
text.formatted: In paediatric implant candidates, brain abnormalities, mostly whitematter changes but also ventriculomegaly and other structural lesions, are common on pre-implant scans <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hong et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Moon et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Xu et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In implanted children, these findings are not inert.

Children with brain lesions were shown to progress over two years, though their performance remained below that of matched implanted controls, which led to the suggestion that pre-operative MRI could help anticipate poor outcomes (Moon et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Children with brain lesions were shown to progress over two years, though their performance remained below that of matched implanted controls, which led to the suggestion that pre-operative MRI could help anticipate poor outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Moon et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Central nervous system anomalies were likewise a negative prognostic factor in a large Italian series, even though good outcomes remained possible (Busi et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Central nervous system anomalies were likewise a negative prognostic factor in a large Italian series, even though good outcomes remained possible <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Busi et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond imaging, many children with hearing loss have additional disabilities, and the type of disability shapes their language outcomes (Cupples et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Beyond imaging, many children with hearing loss have additional disabilities, and the type of disability shapes their language outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Cupples et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Two consequences follow.
The first concerns patients.
When MRI is acquired, a white-matter change or an enlarged ventricle that does not contraindicate implantation rarely enters the outcome model.

In older adults, whose scans would carry the vascular and atrophic changes documented in population imaging, imaging is often limited to the temporal bone and internal auditory canals, so the question is never asked.
The second concerns controls.
Normal-hearing participants in vocoder studies and imaging comparisons are typically screened by questionnaire and audiogram, not by cognitive testing or a radiological read.
Given how common incidental findings are even among young volunteers, few control groups will be entirely free of them.
Most of those findings will be irrelevant to auditory processing.
But no one checks which, and in group designs the control average is the baseline against which patients' reorganization is defined.
For older candidates, now a growing share of implant caseloads, hidden brain variability is not merely background noise.
It is partly produced by the very condition that brings them to the clinic.

In longitudinal MRI studies of older adults, hearing impairment was associated with accelerated wholebrain atrophy and faster volume loss in the right temporal lobe (Lin et al., 2014), and hearing measured in midlife predicted steeper late-life decline in temporal grey matter, the hippocampus and the entorhinal cortex (Armstrong et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In longitudinal MRI studies of older adults, hearing impairment was associated with accelerated wholebrain atrophy and faster volume loss in the right temporal lobe <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Lin et al., 2014)</ref>, and hearing measured in midlife predicted steeper late-life decline in temporal grey matter, the hippocampus and the entorhinal cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Armstrong et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The temporal cortex carries speech and voice processing; the hippocampus and entorhinal cortex support the associative learning that implant users rely on to map new electrical patterns onto familiar words.
The networks that must adapt to the implant are among those most exposed to hearing-related decline.
Epidemiology also frames the stakes.
The latest Lancet Commission ranks hearing loss among the leading potentially modifiable risk factors for dementia (Livingston et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The latest Lancet Commission ranks hearing loss among the leading potentially modifiable risk factors for dementia <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Livingston et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Such estimates may assume causality, but the mechanism remains debated.
A randomized trial adds a lesson that matters directly for implant research.

In older adults with untreated hearing loss, a hearing intervention did not slow cognitive decline overall, but it did so substantially in a pre-specified subgroup with more risk factors and lower baseline cognition (Lin et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In older adults with untreated hearing loss, a hearing intervention did not slow cognitive decline overall, but it did so substantially in a pre-specified subgroup with more risk factors and lower baseline cognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Lin et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The response to restoring hearing depended on the state of the brain receiving it.
Implant data show the same heterogeneity.

Before implantation, a large proportion of older candidates scored abnormally on cognitive testing; a year later, most of them had improved, yet some of those with the best initial profiles showed a slight decline (Mosnier et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Before implantation, a large proportion of older candidates scored abnormally on cognitive testing; a year later, most of them had improved, yet some of those with the best initial profiles showed a slight decline <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Mosnier et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: The improvement suggests that much of the deficit reflected deprivation rather than fixed disease.
Thus, some brains recover with sound; others continue on a separate trajectory that a speech score alone cannot reveal.
If the state of the brain shapes outcome, cognitive measures taken before surgery should carry prognostic information.
They do, though less cleanly than one can suggest.

Pre-operative verbal learning and speechreading skill were shown to predict much of the individual improvement in word recognition after activation (Heydebrand et al., 2007), and pre-operative long-term memory was associated with later speech perception in noise in older recipients (Mosnier et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Pre-operative verbal learning and speechreading skill were shown to predict much of the individual improvement in word recognition after activation <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Heydebrand et al., 2007)</ref>, and pre-operative long-term memory was associated with later speech perception in noise in older recipients <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Mosnier et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Contributions of working memory, inhibition and nonverbal reasoning have been documented in postlingually deaf adults, and it has been argued that poor performers deserve a diagnostic workup of their own (Moberly et al., 2016; Pisoni et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Contributions of working memory, inhibition and nonverbal reasoning have been documented in postlingually deaf adults, and it has been argued that poor performers deserve a diagnostic workup of their own <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Moberly et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Pisoni et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The evidence also carries an honest caveat.
In postlingually deaf adults, Holden et al. (2013) found cognition positively related to word recognition, but the effect disappeared once age at implantation was controlled.
text.formatted: In postlingually deaf adults, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Holden et al. (2013)</ref> found cognition positively related to word recognition, but the effect disappeared once age at implantation was controlled.

text.text: That result is often read as showing that cognition does not matter.
It can equally be read as showing that age is a proxy for something cognitive and structural that the study did not measure directly.
The instruments are part of the problem.

A systematic review found that no cognitive screening tool had been validated for adults with postlingual hearing loss, and that the auditory components of these tools may depress scores in exactly this population, although the evidence on this point was mixed (Raymond et al., 2021).
text.formatted: A systematic review found that no cognitive screening tool had been validated for adults with postlingual hearing loss, and that the auditory components of these tools may depress scores in exactly this population, although the evidence on this point was mixed <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Raymond et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Screening a deaf candidate with a test administered by voice confounds the predictor with the condition being treated.
Even a valid cognitive score has a deeper limitation.
It cannot distinguish a reversible deprivation effect, the kind that improved in most older recipients after implantation, from fixed structural pathology that will not respond to sound.
Only the combination of cognitive testing with structural imaging can separate the two, and that combination is almost never part of candidacy assessment.
A further gap concerns what is tested.
The domains examined so far, such as verbal learning, working memory, inhibition and reasoning, all contribute to prediction, but none of them measures it.

Yet prediction is, we argue, the operation through which the brain restores a degraded signal (Section 2), and predictive models are thought to be embedded in brain activity even at rest (Strelnikov, 2026).
text.formatted: Yet prediction is, we argue, the operation through which the brain restores a degraded signal (Section 2), and predictive models are thought to be embedded in brain activity even at rest <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Strelnikov, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: There should therefore be a dedicated effort to develop tests of predictive brain capacity.
To be usable before implantation, such tests must not depend on hearing.

They could measure how well a person anticipates the continuation of visual or written sequences, how much a predictable context speeds and supports recognition, or how strongly the brain responds when an expected event fails to occur.

Audiovisual paradigms in which a speaker's facial expression predicts forthcoming vocal emphasis (Strelnikov et al., 2015) could then follow how prediction is rebuilt with the implant after activation.
text.formatted: Audiovisual paradigms in which a speaker's facial expression predicts forthcoming vocal emphasis <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Strelnikov et al., 2015)</ref> could then follow how prediction is rebuilt with the implant after activation.

text.text: If predictions are embedded in resting activity, a resting-state sequence added to an existing pre-implant scan might also provide a task-free index.
None of these is yet a validated clinical tool for implant candidates, and developing them is a research perspective.
Human cohorts cannot separate hidden brain pathology from everything that travels with hearing loss: age, vascular risk, duration of deprivation, education.
A controlled animal case can.

The marmoset has been established as a primate model for implant neurophysiology, with single-neuron recordings from the auditory cortex of awake, unilaterally implanted animals (Johnson et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The marmoset has been established as a primate model for implant neurophysiology, with single-neuron recordings from the auditory cortex of awake, unilaterally implanted animals <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Johnson et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: However, the same concern of brain variability exists in animal models. Sadoun et al. (2015) trained young laboratory-bred marmosets on cognitive tasks, and one animal judged healthy by standard veterinary examination and showing no external signs, learned far more slowly than her peers.
text.formatted: However, the same concern of brain variability exists in animal models. <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Sadoun et al. (2015)</ref> trained young laboratory-bred marmosets on cognitive tasks, and one animal judged healthy by standard veterinary examination and showing no external signs, learned far more slowly than her peers.

text.text: Because structural MRI had been scheduled for the study, an explanation was found: a marked enlargement of the temporal horn of the right lateral ventricle, with mild atrophy of the adjacent hippocampus, unchanged on a scan a year later.

Temporal-horn enlargement with hippocampal volume loss lies in the medial temporal territory where hearing-related atrophy has been found in humans (Armstrong et al., 2019; Lin et al., 2014), and ventriculomegaly is among the lesions reported in implanted children (Moon et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Temporal-horn enlargement with hippocampal volume loss lies in the medial temporal territory where hearing-related atrophy has been found in humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Armstrong et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lin et al., 2014)</ref>, and ventriculomegaly is among the lesions reported in implanted children <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Moon et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Had this animal been enrolled in an implant study, it would have been recorded as a poor performer, and the explanation would have defaulted to the device, the surgery or the deprivation.
Thus, an outlier with no other explanation should prompt imaging, or the study risks experimental bias.
Other animal models are also concerned, clinically silent ventriculomegaly is common in some laboratory rat populations (Tu et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Other animal models are also concerned, clinically silent ventriculomegaly is common in some laboratory rat populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Tu et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In children, hidden brain variability is both more common and harder to see.
Brain findings are relatively frequent on pre-implant scans, and additional disabilities are reported in an important part of deaf children (Section 4).
Yet cognition is still developing, adult screening tools do not apply, and a slow trajectory can be attributed to age at implantation for years before anyone looks further.

Electrophysiological work has shown a sensitive period for central auditory development, with cortical responses more likely to mature normally when implantation occurs early in childhood (Sharma et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Electrophysiological work has shown a sensitive period for central auditory development, with cortical responses more likely to mature normally when implantation occurs early in childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Sharma et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: A sensitive period sharpens the cost of an unrecognized confound: a child whose poor progress reflects a structural problem may be pushed toward more intensive auditory therapy when a different plan is needed.
Even in carefully selected groups, individual variation is large.
In the everyday-sound sorting study, both implanted and normal-hearing children showed considerable variation in how they grouped sounds (Berland et al., 2019).
text.formatted: In the everyday-sound sorting study, both implanted and normal-hearing children showed considerable variation in how they grouped sounds <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Berland et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Without a structural or cognitive baseline, there is no way to tell how much of the spread within the implanted group reflects deafness, and how much reflects the ordinary heterogeneity of developing brains.
Single-sided deafness raises the stakes further.
In these children, one ear is normal; what fails is central integration of the two ears for localization and listening in noise.

In adults with acquired asymmetric hearing loss, PET imaging has linked cortical plasticity after implantation to spatial hearing (Karoui et al., 2023), and EEG work in adults with unilateral loss has related brain plasticity to spatial adaptation (Alzaher et al., 2023); whether the same holds in children is not yet known.
text.formatted: In adults with acquired asymmetric hearing loss, PET imaging has linked cortical plasticity after implantation to spatial hearing <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Karoui et al., 2023)</ref>, and EEG work in adults with unilateral loss has related brain plasticity to spatial adaptation <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Alzaher et al., 2023)</ref>; whether the same holds in children is not yet known.

text.text: Outcome in single-sided deafness is close to a pure test of the central auditory system.
fNIRS, being non-invasive and little affected by movement, has been proposed for studying children with single-sided deafness (Calmels et al., 2022).
text.formatted: fNIRS, being non-invasive and little affected by movement, has been proposed for studying children with single-sided deafness <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Calmels et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, fNIRS samples the cortical surface; it cannot see a ventricle or a hippocampus.
MRI is already used to look for inner-ear and cochlear-nerve anomalies in children with sensorineural loss, and such anomalies are more frequent in unilateral loss (McClay et al., 2008).
text.formatted: MRI is already used to look for inner-ear and cochlear-nerve anomalies in children with sensorineural loss, and such anomalies are more frequent in unilateral loss <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(McClay et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Quantifying the brain on those existing scans, and adding a brief non-auditory cognitive measure, would turn studies like this one into tests of the hidden-variability hypothesis at almost no extra cost.

Most incidental findings call for no immediate action: very few required intervention in a large population imaging study, although their natural course remains uncertain (Vernooij et al., 2007), and a metaanalysis concluded that incidental findings do not justify screening healthy people (Morris et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Most incidental findings call for no immediate action: very few required intervention in a large population imaging study, although their natural course remains uncertain <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Vernooij et al., 2007)</ref>, and a metaanalysis concluded that incidental findings do not justify screening healthy people <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Morris et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: But the claim here is not that each finding matters clinically.
It is that unmeasured brain variability sits inside outcome models as noise, and that quantifying it is the only way to learn which findings matter for implant use and which do not.
Reorganization predicts that the informative signal lies in deprived auditory and visual regions and scales with duration of deafness.
General integrity predicts that it lies in regions deafness did not alter, in hippocampal and frontal systems, and in measures that would predict learning in any domain.
The result of Feng et al. (2018) fits the second pattern.
text.formatted: The result of <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Feng et al. (2018)</ref> fits the second pattern.

text.text: Both mechanisms can operate at once, and a design that measures both can apportion the variance.

Age is a population-level proxy. Holden et al. (2013) found that cognition no longer predicted word recognition once age at implantation was taken into account; in a model where age stands in for brain state, that is expected.
text.formatted: Age is a population-level proxy. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Holden et al. (2013)</ref> found that cognition no longer predicted word recognition once age at implantation was taken into account; in a model where age stands in for brain state, that is expected.

text.text: A direct structural and cognitive measure should outperform it at the individual level, and that is a testable claim.
Screening should not be used to refuse implants, and the evidence argues against using brain measures as gatekeepers.
Most cognitively impaired older candidates improved after implantation (Mosnier et al., 2015), and children with brain lesions still progressed (Moon et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Most cognitively impaired older candidates improved after implantation <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Mosnier et al., 2015)</ref>, and children with brain lesions still progressed <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Moon et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The purpose of phenotyping is counselling, rehabilitation planning and honest expectations, not exclusion.
A candidate with hippocampal atrophy deserves an implant and a rehabilitation programme designed for slower associative learning.
MRI is expensive but many candidates a brain MRI is already being acquired, and volumetric quantification of an existing scan is a software step.
The marginal cost is small compared with the device and lifetime care.
The remedy is not a new technology.
It is a change in what implant programmes and implant studies routinely record.
Measure cognition with tools built for hearing loss.

Adult candidates should complete a short cognitive assessment that does not depend on audition, such as the MoCA-H, a visual version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (Dawes et al., 2023; Völter et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Adult candidates should complete a short cognitive assessment that does not depend on audition, such as the MoCA-H, a visual version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dawes et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Völter et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Scores belong in the outcome database, not only in the clinical notes.
Develop tests of predictive capacity.
We propose that the brain restores the degraded implant signal in large part by prediction, yet no test targets this capacity.

Since predictive models are thought to be maintained continuously in brain activity (Strelnikov, 2026), a coordinated effort should develop and validate non-auditory tests of predictive brain capacity, behavioral and electrophysiological, for adults and for children, and add them to candidacy assessment and outcome databases alongside cognitive scores.
text.formatted: Since predictive models are thought to be maintained continuously in brain activity <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Strelnikov, 2026)</ref>, a coordinated effort should develop and validate non-auditory tests of predictive brain capacity, behavioral and electrophysiological, for adults and for children, and add them to candidacy assessment and outcome databases alongside cognitive scores.

text.text: Where pre-implant MRI is acquired, add an automated volumetric read of the hippocampus, lateral ventricles, temporal lobes and white-matter lesion load, referenced to age norms.
Where imaging is limited to the temporal bone, a brief whole-brain structural sequence is worth considering, particularly in candidates over 60.4.
Code incidental findings as variables.
A white-matter change or ventricular enlargement that does not contraindicate surgery should still be recorded in a structured way, so that its relation to outcome can be estimated across centres.
Give poor performers a structured workup.

Patients below the expected trajectory at 6 to 12 months should be reassessed for device, fitting and surgical causes and, as has already been urged for poor performers, for cognitive ones (Moberly et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Patients below the expected trajectory at 6 to 12 months should be reassessed for device, fitting and surgical causes and, as has already been urged for poor performers, for cognitive ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Moberly et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Hold controls to the same standard.
Normal-hearing controls in vocoder and imaging studies should receive the same cognitive screen and, where MRI is acquired, the same radiological and volumetric read.
Exclusions and their reasons should be reported.
Pool the data.
Multicentre pooling has already shown what it can do for clinical predictors (Blamey et al., 2013).
text.formatted: Multicentre pooling has already shown what it can do for clinical predictors <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Blamey et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: A registry adding cognitive and volumetric variables would show, within a few years, how much of the missing variance belongs to the brain.
Imaging in animal models.

In marmoset and other primate implant studies, any behavioural outlier should undergo structural MRI, since an unexplained learning deficit can reflect an unsuspected brain abnormality (Sadoun et al., 2015); ideally, a baseline scan should be standard before animals are allocated to conditions.
text.formatted: In marmoset and other primate implant studies, any behavioural outlier should undergo structural MRI, since an unexplained learning deficit can reflect an unsuspected brain abnormality <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Sadoun et al., 2015)</ref>; ideally, a baseline scan should be standard before animals are allocated to conditions.

text.text: The central prediction of this article is falsifiable.

If hidden brain variability matters, adding cognitive and volumetric measures to the established clinical model should raise explained variance in a large cohort, and should do so most among the poorest performers.
The same logic applies to predictive capacity: once validated, a dedicated test should explain outcome variance beyond what general cognitive scores capture.
Decades after cochlear implants became standard care, the field still cannot say in advance which patients will struggle.
It has examined the cochlea, the electrode and the history of deafness in detail, and crossmodal reorganization with real ingenuity.
It has examined least the general condition of the brain that must do the learning.
The human evidence now makes that omission hard to defend.
Outcome measures depend on prediction, multisensory integration and categorization, all central operations.
Prediction has a special place among them, because it is how the brain supplies what the implant fails to deliver, yet no dedicated test of it exists.
"Normal" brains frequently carry structural findings, and implant candidates carry more of them.
Hearing loss itself tracks with temporal and hippocampal atrophy, and cognition predicts outcome when it is measured with appropriate tools.
The proposal of the article is to measure the brain the implant depends on, including its capacity to predict, in patients and in controls, before deciding what the remaining variance means.
